name: Accentuation effect
statement: Putting a two-class label on a graded series makes people judge the two items either side of the class boundary as further apart than they are.
meaning: The claim is about judged differences, not about liking. A perceiver estimates the magnitude of each item in a series, and the estimates stretch at the point where one class ends and the other begins. Nothing in the claim requires the classes to be groups of people, and nothing requires the perceiver to prefer one class. Tajfel and Wilkes state two predictions taken from Tajfel's 1959 paper. A classification that runs consistently with the physical dimension shifts judgements of magnitude in the direction the class membership implies. A classification unrelated to the dimension does nothing. Beside the between-class stretch they derive a within-class squeeze: items inside a class should be judged more alike. Two subsidiary hypotheses follow. A more salient classification should strengthen both effects, and so should repeated experience of the classification. The between-class half is the one usually meant by the name. The within-class half is the one that connects the idea to stereotyping, and it is the weaker of the two.

origin.who: Henri Tajfel and A. L. Wilkes
origin.note: 'Classification and quantitative judgement' was received on 24 July 1962 and published in the May 1963 issue, from the Department of Social and Administrative Studies at Oxford. The predictions it tested were set out four years earlier in Tajfel's 'Quantitative judgement in social perception', and the 1963 paper quotes them from pages 20 to 21 of that article. Tajfel and Wilkes describe their own experiments as 'a simplified exercise in stereotyping'.

evidence: Eight lines differed from each other by a constant ratio of about 5% of length. The shortest was 16.2 cm; the text gives the longest as 22.9 cm while the table of actual values ends at 22.8. Each line was drawn diagonally on a sheet of white cardboard 63.5 cm by 50.8 cm, and a separate sheet was made for every presentation. Sixty-one volunteers from Oxford University, Westminster Training College and Manchester University took part in the first two experiments, and 54 came back a week later. Group C, twelve people, saw the four shorter lines labelled A and the four longer labelled B. Group R, thirteen people, saw the same letters alternating at random. Group U, twelve people, saw no letters. A second experiment repeated the classified and unlabelled conditions with twelve people each under a different mode of prior presentation. Lines were shown one at a time, six times, in successive random orders, at about 8 ft, with judgements called out in centimetres. The boundary sat between stimuli 4 and 5. In the first sessions the apparent difference there was 100% greater than the actual difference for the classified groups and 11% greater for the controls; in the second sessions, 122% and 44%. Fitting a linear function to each subject's judgements within each class gave mean inter-class differences of 1.9 for the classified groups against 1.1 for both control groups, rising to 2.1 against 1.4 and 1.1 a week later. The analysis of variance gave F = 6.12, P < 0.025 for the classification in the first sessions and F = 4.40, P < 0.05 in the second. Two controls rule out the letters themselves. In group R the mean judgements of a stimulus labelled A and labelled B were practically identical. Mean adjacent differences were 1.07 when both items carried the same letter and 1.12 when they carried different ones. The effect appeared at one place only. An analysis run on the other point where the classified groups exaggerated a gap, between stimuli 1 and 2, gave F = 0.47 for the classification.

examples.tag: The lines labelled A and B
examples.text: Eight lines grow steadily in length, and the four shorter ones carry one label while the four longer carry another. Asked to estimate each line, people leave a bigger gap between the fourth and the fifth than between any other neighbouring pair.

examples.tag: The mark either side of a pass
examples.text: Marks run in a smooth series and a pass mark cuts them in two. Two scripts a single point apart are judged far apart in quality when the line falls between them, and much alike when it does not. Nothing about the scripts has changed.

examples.tag: The towns either side of a county line
examples.text: Two towns twenty miles apart on the same side of a boundary are described as neighbours. Two towns the same distance apart with the line running between them are placed in different parts of the country.

replication.headline: Direct line-judgement replications in 2002 and 2021 found the between-class stretch, but only under uncertainty about the judgement scale, and the within-class half appeared in the original only after repeated judging.
replication.detail: Tajfel and Wilkes obtained the between-class result at once and the within-class one only later. Their analysis of mean intra-class slopes showed that neither the classification nor its salience changed the apparent differences within a class. They write that this does not confirm the prediction that classifying would increase the judged similarity of stimuli in the same class. Salience made no difference, and neither did returning a week later. Repeated judging inside a single session did. Over the last five of eleven presentations the classified group's inter-class difference was 2.0, against 0.7 for the random-label group and 0.9 for the unlabelled group. Those gaps reached P < 0.001 and P < 0.01, and the classified group's intra-class slope fell to 0.83 against 0.99 and 1.02. Measured as the shift from the first six presentations to the last five, that flattening of the slope was significant against each control group at P < 0.01. The matching stability of the inter-class difference did not quite reach P = 0.05. The authors' fifth conclusion is that repeated experience within a session brings a definite increase in the judged similarity of stimuli in the same class. Corneille, Klein, Lambert and Judd rebuilt the task for Belgian and American participants estimating lines in inches or in centimetres. Their abstract reports accentuation higher when the lines were systematically categorised, and stronger when the unit was the unfamiliar one. It closes by saying the finding may help explain why researchers had had difficulty replicating the effect in the past. Foroni and Rothbart, reading that paper, put it more sharply in a footnote: it replicated Tajfel and Wilkes only with judgement scales unfamiliar to the participants. Drače and Čehajić ran the closest recent direct replication, with 136 of 139 psychology undergraduates at Sarajevo analysed, assigned to no-label, label, or label plus a fear induction. Eight on-screen lines ran from 7.4 cm to 11.4 cm, each judged six times, and the accentuation score was the mean estimated difference between the two lines flanking the boundary. Means were 0.67 cm with no labels, SD 0.40, 0.89 cm with labels, SD 0.51, and 1.04 cm with labels plus fear, SD 0.53. The planned contrast that reached significance set label-plus-fear against no-label, F(1, 133) = 12.48, p = .001, partial eta squared .08; the orthogonal contrast testing residual variance was F < 1. No test of labels against no labels on its own is reported in that paper. Sample size was fixed in advance at 135 for 80% power against a medium effect. Away from lines the picture splits by measure. Foroni and Rothbart showed 233 people nine female silhouettes graded by ponderosity and imposed labels between phases. Labels increased within-category similarity, F(1, 230) = 11.01, p = .001, eta squared .05, while the matching accentuation of across-category pairs reached only F(1, 230) = 3.26, p = .07, eta squared .014. On absolute weight estimates both held: assimilation at F(1, 230) = 8.59, p = .004, and accentuation at F(1, 230) = 8.98, p = .003. McGarty and Penny had 55 people judge political statements classified by author and found both halves, and their abstract says this was unlike numerous other studies with similar designs. Rothermund and Deutsch report two preregistered experiments in which perceivers exaggerated differences between two fictitious groups, with accentuation stronger for the group met second and still present for the group met first.

study.cite: Drače, S., & Čehajić, M. (2021). Emotional Determinants of Categorical Accentuation. Psihologijske teme, 30(2), 271-278.

limits: The original is small and old. Sixty-one volunteers were split into groups of twelve and thirteen, the paper reports F ratios and P values with no effect sizes and no confidence intervals, and nothing about it was preregistered. Its own comparison of the classified group against the random-label group, the cleanest control it had, missed significance in the first session and reached P < 0.01 only in the second. Scoring each subject by the mean of his two sessions, the same comparison reaches P < 0.025. Tajfel and Wilkes note the asymmetry themselves: the random-label group existed in one experiment and not the other, because enough subjects could not be found. Where the effect shows up seems to depend on how uncertain the judgement is. Corneille and colleagues found it stronger in an unfamiliar measurement unit, and Drače and Čehajić found it stronger after a fear induction, which is consistent with an effect that needs room in the scale to appear. The line task itself is unusual in that respect. Tajfel and Wilkes had British subjects in 1962 judge in centimetres and showed them a ruler with examples of the relation between centimetres and inches, which is the detail Corneille and colleagues built their replication around. No pooled estimate across studies was located, and no multi-laboratory replication was located. Three papers cited here were not read in full. Corneille, Klein, Lambert and Judd is closed at Unpaywall and at the publisher, so everything attributed to it comes from its abstract or from Foroni and Rothbart's footnote. McGarty and Penny is cited from the abstract Crossref carries. OpenAlex, Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar all record Rothermund and Deutsch as open at the publisher, but the journal's host answered every request with a bot challenge, so only the abstract was read. Europe PMC lists that same paper as subscription only, which shows how far one index can sit from another. Carter and Schooler was read in full from the Internet Archive scan of the July 1949 issue of Psychological Review. Searches on 21 September 2026 covered Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, PubMed, Europe PMC, Hrčak, the Internet Archive, ULB DI-fusion, the authors' university pages and the open web. UCLouvain DIAL refused every connection on that date.
misreadings: The effect is read as a claim about attitude. It is a claim about judged magnitude, and the same stretch at a boundary appears for lines, weights and political statements. This atlas keeps the out-group homogeneity effect as a separate entry, no. 208, for the same reason, and the two claims are related without being the same one. Out-group homogeneity is the within-class half of Tajfel's hypothesis applied to people, and the classification on its own did not produce that half in 1963. Entry 208 carries the pooled estimate and the record of the measures that support it. Presenting the 1963 lines study as the demonstration of out-group homogeneity gets the direction of support backwards. The second confusion is with Bruner and Goodman's coin studies, which are a different claim with a different design. Thirty ten-year-olds sat in front of an adjustable circle of light and turned a knob to match it to an object. Twenty of them, ten rich and ten poor, judged coins. A separate control group of ten judged grey cardboard discs of the same size, so no child judged both. Coins were judged larger than discs, the overestimation grew with the value of the coin apart from the half dollar, and the poor children overestimated more than the rich ones. That is value inflating perceived size, with no category boundary and no series to stretch. Bruner and Goodman use the word accentuate for it, which is part of why the two get bundled, and their rich group over-judged a half dollar by 17.4% with the coin in view and 34.7% from memory. Carter and Schooler repeated the experiment two years later on 48 children aged nine to eleven, each of whom judged coins from memory, coins in view, aluminium discs and cardboard discs. With the coins in view the rich and poor groups did not differ, and the gap between them appeared only in the memory judgements. Small discs were generally underestimated and large ones overestimated, whatever they were made of. Their summary doubts that value organises the perception of objects that are plainly there. Third, retellings say the classified series was judged more different throughout. Tajfel and Wilkes found the difference only at the break between stimuli 4 and 5, and reported F = 0.47 for the classification at the other point where the classified groups stretched a gap. Fourth, the lines are often described as vertical. The paper says each was drawn diagonally, on a large sheet chosen to keep the frame from giving the differences away.

sources.text: Tajfel, H., & Wilkes, A. L. (1963). Classification and quantitative judgement. British Journal of Psychology, 54(2), 101-114. The founding paper. Read in full from a scanned copy hosted by the University of Western Macedonia; source for every figure attributed to the original here.

Tajfel, H. (1959). Quantitative judgement in social perception. British Journal of Psychology, 50(1), 16-29. The paper that stated the predictions. Closed at Unpaywall on 21 September 2026 and not read; it is listed because Tajfel and Wilkes quote its pages 20 to 21 and 23 for the hypotheses they test.

Corneille, O., Klein, O., Lambert, S., & Judd, C. M. (2002). On the role of familiarity with units of measurement in categorical accentuation: Tajfel and Wilkes (1963) revisited and replicated. Psychological Science, 13(4), 380-383. Closed at Unpaywall and at the publisher on 21 September 2026, with no repository copy found. The abstract was read at PubMed and at Crossref and matched; no number from this paper appears on this page.

Drače, S., & Čehajić, M. (2021). Emotional Determinants of Categorical Accentuation. Psihologijske teme, 30(2), 271-278. Read in full from the open-access copy at Hrčak. Source for the 136 participants, the condition means and the planned contrasts.

Foroni, F., & Rothbart, M. (2011). Category boundaries and category labels: When does a category name influence the perceived similarity of category members? Social Cognition, 29(5), 547-576. Read in full from the copy hosted at SISSA. Source for the silhouette experiments and for the footnote reading of Corneille and colleagues.

McGarty, C., & Penny, R. E. C. (1988). Categorization, accentuation and social judgement. British Journal of Social Psychology, 27(2), 147-157. Abstract read at Crossref; source for the 55 subjects, for both halves of the effect appearing, and for the remark that this was unlike numerous other studies with similar designs. Full text not obtained on 21 September 2026.

Rothermund, P., & Deutsch, R. (2024). Exaggerating differences back and forth: Two levels of intergroup accentuation. British Journal of Social Psychology, 63(2), 708-722. Abstract read at Europe PMC and at Crossref. Three indexes record the published version as open at the publisher, but the journal's host met every request on 21 September 2026 with a bot challenge, so the full text was not read and no figure here comes from it.

Bruner, J. S., & Goodman, C. C. (1947). Value and need as organizing factors in perception. The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 42(1), 33-44. Read in full from the Classics in the History of Psychology transcription at York University. Source for the coin study's design and results, which this page cites only to separate them from the accentuation effect.

Carter, L. F., & Schooler, K. (1949). Value, need, and other factors in perception. Psychological Review, 56(4), 200-207. The contemporaneous re-examination of the coin studies. Read in full from the Internet Archive scan of the issue, which carries no separate abstract. Source for the 48 children, the four judgement conditions and the summary.
